readMe.title: China Defense-Industrial Atlas — Supplier Scorecards v1.2
readMe.blurb: Additive, source-gated supplier × capability assessments through 2026-08-31. This workbook preserves the legacy Atlas as context and does not replace its broader research-priority ranking.

notes.note: The unit of analysis is a supplier × capability family, not a corporate family or product brand. A parent’s strategic importance does not make every affiliate a technical supplier.

Systemic importance combines criticality, production maturity, cross-domain leverage, and technical frontier. The evidence-qualified lower bound discounts weaker evidence. It is a research triage score—not spend, valuation, targeting value, or sanctions advice.
Criticality 4 requires explicit sole/limited-source or requalification language. Only scores supported by that threshold receive a substitution-risk assessment; blank means unknown, not low risk.

Completed production-enabling awards (robotics, test, CNC, validation) are separated from mission-component suppliers. A shipyard robotics award is meaningful industrial-base evidence, not proof of a weapons-subsystem relationship.

PLA candidate notices, company marketing, and comparative tests are preserved as watchlist evidence. They do not enter the verified leaderboard until a final award, delivery, qualification, or other stronger evidence is found.
Foreign-dependency rows are tagged by directness and currentness. Historical export-control cases are not silently converted into current defense-program vulnerabilities.
For the full claim ledger and source detail, use the accompanying v1.2 SQLite database or the Atlas site’s Supplier scorecards tab.

scoringMethod.blurb: Inputs are transparent. The v1.2 initial rankings use the displayed weights; scenario columns in Scorecard Ranking allow sensitivity checks but do not silently re-sort the frozen research triage order.

chart.plain: A working chart of the capability nodes a robotic or unmanned military system depends on, from sensors to production tooling. Each node lists the firms the scorecard package evidences against it. A node with no evidence is shown as empty, not filled by inference.

rows.cautious_inference: This is evidence of a research/test integration demand for an open and model-rich quadruped platform rather than a simple off-the-shelf patrol robot
rows.does_not_establish: It does not name a supplier or show a purchase fielding deployment or operational use
rows.recommended_use: Trend card: supervised embodied-robot experimentation; keep separate from completed procurements

rows.signal: PLA procurement intention exposes a commercial FPV component stack
rows.confirmed_fact: A PLA procurement-intent notice names and quantifies individual FPV items including a RUSHFPV STM32F722 flight controller BLHeli ESC TBS UNIFY video transmitter Foxeer camera RadioMaster RP1/2 ELRS receiver and Tattu R-Line battery
rows.cautious_inference: The source is a strong public indicator of interest in an interoperable low-cost FPV stack and useful for a component/dependency map
rows.does_not_establish: It is an intention not an award; it does not show that every named brand was bought deployed at scale or indispensable to a military supply chain
rows.recommended_use: Add as a demand and foreign-origin/component-topology signal with non-award status

rows.signal: C-UAS performance evidence is broad not concentrated
rows.confirmed_fact: China Security Association and public-security partners report 26 firms in a three-batch 15-day portable C-UAS comparison and list 21 as excellent performers
rows.cautious_inference: The portable-C-UAS vendor layer appears competitively broad; a single test certificate should usually increase capability confidence more than criticality
rows.does_not_establish: It does not measure market share production scale military acceptance or comparative rank within the 21
rows.recommended_use: Use as a concentration/substitutability control in C-UAS scorecards

bibliography.what_it_is_good_for: Named product categories, batch production, customer class, qualifications, capacity, and sometimes limited-source language.
bibliography.what_it_cannot_prove_alone: A generic ‘special market’ disclosure does not identify a program, military buyer, monopoly, or delivery event.

bibliography.what_it_is_good_for: Named winner, buyer, project scope, result state, date, and disclosed price for specific production or equipment procurements.
bibliography.what_it_cannot_prove_alone: A shipyard production-equipment award does not establish a weapon component relationship or enterprise-wide revenue.

bibliography.what_it_is_good_for: Demand shape, technical requirements, bid/pre-award/final-state distinctions, and named component stacks.
bibliography.what_it_cannot_prove_alone: Intent, candidates, or first-ranked notices cannot be treated as award, delivery, fielding, or repeat supply without final proof.

bibliography.what_it_is_good_for: Attributed capability, provenance, local incubation, test participation, and sometimes installed-base claims.
bibliography.what_it_cannot_prove_alone: They are not independent evidence of contract completion, program integration, or production volumes when claims are company-attributed.

bibliography.what_it_is_good_for: Named historical exports/reexports, tools, direct counterparties, values, and known time windows.
bibliography.what_it_cannot_prove_alone: They do not establish current access, a specific Chinese fab/program, defense end use, or a present vulnerability without additional evidence.

bibliography.what_it_is_good_for: Capability cohort breadth and comparative test outcomes useful for market-structure inference.
bibliography.what_it_cannot_prove_alone: An ‘excellent’ result is not procurement, irreplacability, or operational deployment; a broad cohort often points toward higher substitutability.
